The first article discusses a study on characterizing political fake news on Twitter through meta-data analysis. The researchers collected over 1.5 million tweets on the day of the US presidential election and analyzed their meta-data to identify differences between tweets containing fake news and those not containing them. The study found significant differences in the distribution of followers, the number of URLs on tweets, and the verification of users. The researchers also identified three dimensions that may help distinguish fake news from legit information: exposure, characterization, and polarization.

The second article presents a study on language identification using multiple pooling strategies. The researchers explored different pooling strategies, including NetVLAD, Ghost-VLAD, statistic pooling, and average pooling. They used a dataset of 635 hours of audio data for 7 Indian languages and compared the performance of different models. The results showed that Ghost-VLAD pooling outperformed all other pooling methods, achieving an accuracy of 98.24%.

The third article discusses a study on speech emotion recognition using a deep dual recurrent encoder model. The researchers proposed a novel model that simultaneously utilizes audio and text data to recognize emotions from speech. They used the IEMOCAP dataset and compared the performance of different models. The results showed that the proposed model outperformed previous state-of-the-art methods, achieving a weighted average precision (WAP) value of 0.718.

The fourth article presents a study on abusive language detection using different learning models. The researchers compared the accuracy of different models, including traditional machine learning classifiers and neural network-based models. The results showed that bidirectional GRU networks with Latent Topic Clustering (LTC) provided the most accurate results in detecting abusive language.

The fifth article discusses a study on emotion recognition using Facebook reactions as proxies for emotion labels. The researchers trained a set of Support Vector Machine models for emotion recognition using Facebook reactions as labels. The results showed that the models achieved competitive or even state-of-the-art results for some of the emotion labels on existing, standard evaluation datasets.

The sixth article presents a study on hashtag segmentation using a pairwise neural ranking approach. The researchers proposed a multi-task pairwise neural ranking approach to better incorporate and distinguish the relative order between candidate segmentations of a given hashtag. They used a dataset of 12,594 unique hashtags and their associated tweets and compared the performance of different models. The results showed that the proposed approach outperformed the state-of-the-art approach, achieving an error reduction of 24.6% on multi-token hashtags.

The seventh article discusses a study on multi-document summarization using a concept-map-based approach. The researchers proposed a novel task, concept-map-based multi-document summarization (MDS), and presented a new crowdsourcing scheme to create reference summaries. They created a new corpus of 30 topics, each with around 40 source documents on educational topics and a summarizing concept map that is the consensus of many crowdworkers. The results showed that the proposed approach outperformed the state-of-the-art approach, achieving a segmentation-level accuracy of 82.1%.

The eighth article presents a study on text summarization using a document-level encoder based on BERT. The researchers proposed a novel document-level encoder based on BERT, which is able to encode a document and obtain representations for its sentences. They used three single-document news summarization datasets and compared the performance of different models. The results showed that the proposed approach outperformed the state-of-the-art approach, achieving state-of-the-art results under both extractive and abstractive settings.
